newsitem.title: JORDAN: Hungry investors want Jordan to release shares.
newsitem.headline: Hungry investors want Jordan to release shares.

text.p: An unprecedented global fund buying spree on Jordanian blue-chip shares can only be sustained by a government sell-off of its sizeable portfolio to alleviate limited supplies, investment managers said on Wednesday.
The sustained emerging fund demand on mainly three mining and cement blue-chips has lifted the stock market to its highest levels since late 1995.
Foreign purchases in the last two weeks alone are close to the whole of last year's buying, totalling 9.6 million dinars, analysts said.

"This could be the year foreigners finally really come to Jordan with substantial sums...but the lack of supply is hampering foreign buying...everybody is talking about the illiquidity of the Jordanian market.." said Ziad Basha, securities manager at Jordan's British Bank of the Middle East.

Availability of more blue-chip stock, in a market which suffers from a limited free float of blue chip shares, now hinges on lifting a 50 percent foreign ownership ceiling and a drive to sell the state's vast stock portfolio.
Many of the firms in demand have limited free floats such as Arab Potash, one of Jordan's top export earners, with only 0.06 percent of its shares freely available for trade.
The state holdings are estimated at around 20 percent of the market's capitalisation of 3.2 billion dinars ($4.5 billion.)

Prices, which have shot up as much as 15 percent on some of the bluechips in demand such as Arab Potash, are moving up much faster than would have been expected because of the tight supply, said Omar al-Masri of Atlas Investment Group.
The official Amman Financial Market index ended the trading week on Wednesday at 158.92 points, its highest level since November 1995.

Samir Jaradat, assistant general manager for investments at Jordan Investment Finance Bank, who is executing many of the emerging funds orders, says he expected prices to continue rising at the current pace of demand.
While local investors are taking a back seat, foreign funds are for the first time major players accounting for at least 70 percent of daily value since they started their buying spree.

The bulk of the buying has been focused in mainly three stock, Jordan Cement, Arab Potash and Jordan Phosphate Mines -- all firms with large state holdings, and seeking million of dollars of funds for major industrial expansion projects.
Funds appear to be positioning themselves ahead of an expected rally once these firms launch GDR (Global Deposit Receipts) listings before year-end, say Masri.
A star performer has been Jordan Cement. The government wants to dispose of a 33 percent stake in the firm's 60 million dinar capital, possibly through a GDR listing.

The heightened foreign interest is underpinned by current price levels which are now more attractive compared to Jordan's regional competitors such as Egypt and Morocco which have witnessed record capital inflows this year.

"In terms of various valuation measures, including price earnings ratio on a relative basis, Jordan now is cheapest," said Masri. Jordan's PE ratio was 10.7 compared to a high 17.3 percent in Morocco and Egypt's 13.3 percent in 1997.
Economic laws passed this month which were applauded by investors as evidence of government seriousness to accelerate opening the economy to foreigners have bolstered confidence.
"After the new laws and the potential for GDRs, foreign investors are much more encouraged than the last few years," said Masri.
